A fungus is a living organism — a life form that is neither a plant, nor an animal, nor a bacterium. It belongs to its own separate kingdom of life, called the Fungi kingdom. The plural of fungus is fungi (pronounced fun-jye or fun-gee), though "funguses" is also acceptable.

Think of a fungus as a living thing that survives by absorbing nutrients from other things — dead wood, soil, food, skin, or even other organisms. Unlike plants, fungi cannot make their own food from sunlight. Unlike animals, they don't hunt or eat. Instead, they release special chemicals called enzymes into whatever they're growing on, break it down, and then soak up the nutrients — almost like digesting food outside their body and then absorbing the result.
What does a fungus look like?

Fungi come in wildly different shapes and sizes, so there isn't one single "look." But most fungi share one structural feature: they are made of thin, thread-like strands called hyphae (singular: hypha). These threads grow and branch out in all directions, forming a tangled web called a mycelium. The mycelium is often hidden — buried in soil, inside rotting wood, or spread through food — and is the main "body" of the fungus doing the work.

What you see above the surface (like a mushroom cap) is not the whole organism — it's just the reproductive part, like a fruit on a tree. The real body is the hidden mycelium underneath.

Some fungi, however, are single-celled and have no visible structure at all — yeasts are a perfect example of this.

Fungi reproduce primarily through spores — tiny, lightweight particles (far smaller than a grain of sand) that are released into the air, water, or soil. When a spore lands in a suitable environment — the right temperature, moisture, and food source — it germinates and grows into a new fungus. This is why mold can appear on bread within days: a few invisible spores landed on it and found exactly what they needed.

Some fungi also reproduce by splitting (in the case of yeast) or by growing new sections from their existing mycelium.

Fungi are found almost everywhere on Earth:

  • In soil — most soil is teeming with fungal mycelium
  • On and inside dead or decaying matter — rotting logs, fallen leaves, old food
  • On living things — on the skin, nails, or inside the body of animals and humans; on the roots or leaves of plants
  • In water — some species live in rivers, lakes, or the ocean
  • In extreme environments — certain fungi survive in deserts, on rocks, and even in radioactive zones

While all fungi share the same basic biology, they vary a great deal in form:

Mushrooms are the most recognizable fungi. The cap-and-stem structure you see is the fruiting body — the spore-producing part. The real organism is the underground mycelium. Some mushrooms are edible (like button mushrooms, shiitake, or portobello), some are medicinal, and some are deadly poisonous.

Molds are multicellular fungi that grow as visible fuzzy or powdery patches — the green or black stuff you see on old bread, fruit, or damp walls. They spread rapidly through spores.

Yeasts are single-celled fungi. They don't form threads or visible structures. They reproduce by budding — a small bud grows off the parent cell and eventually breaks away as a new cell.

Rusts, smuts, and blights are fungi that parasitize plants and cause serious diseases in crops.

Lichens — though technically a partnership between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium — are largely fungal in structure.
The role of fungi in nature

Fungi are among the most important organisms on Earth, primarily because they are decomposers. When a tree falls and dies, when a leaf drops to the ground, when an animal's body is left behind — fungi break it all down. They digest the complex materials (wood, dead tissue, leaves) and return the nutrients locked inside them back to the soil. Without fungi, dead matter would pile up indefinitely and the nutrients inside would never be recycled. In this sense, fungi are essential to the health of every ecosystem on the planet.

Many fungi also form deep partnerships with plants. About 90% of all land plants have fungal networks attached to their roots — a relationship called mycorrhiza. The fungus helps the plant absorb water and minerals from the soil, and in return, the plant shares sugars with the fungus. This partnership is so critical that many plants cannot survive without it.

Beneficial uses:

  • Food: Mushrooms are a major food source worldwide. Yeast is used to make bread rise and to ferment beverages like beer and wine.
  • Medicine: One of the most important antibiotics ever discovered — penicillin — came from a mold called Penicillium. Many other medicines, including immunosuppressants (used after organ transplants), are derived from fungi.
  • Fermentation: Fungi are essential in producing cheese (the blue in blue cheese is a mold), soy sauce, miso, tempeh, and vinegar.
  • Bioremediation: Some fungi can break down pollutants and toxic waste in soil.
  • Research: Yeast has been used extensively as a model organism to study genetics and cell biology.

Harmful effects:

  • Infections in humans: Fungi can infect human skin (athlete's foot, ringworm), nails, hair, mouth (thrush), and in more serious cases, the lungs or bloodstream. These are called fungal infections or mycoses. People with weakened immune systems are especially vulnerable.
  • Crop destruction: Fungi cause enormous damage to agriculture — diseases like wheat rust, potato blight (which caused the Irish Famine in the 1840s), and rice blast devastate crops.
  • Food spoilage: Molds ruin food and can produce toxic chemicals called mycotoxins — like aflatoxin, found in improperly stored grains and nuts, which is one of the most potent natural carcinogens known.
  • Damage to materials: Fungi break down wood, fabric, leather, and even some paints and building materials.

A fungus is a distinct type of living organism — not a plant, not an animal — that feeds by breaking down and absorbing nutrients from other organic matter. Its body is usually a network of microscopic threads called mycelium, spread through soil, wood, or food. It reproduces through spores. Fungi range from microscopic single-celled yeasts to large mushrooms. They play an irreplaceable role in nature as decomposers and as partners to plants. They are also deeply intertwined with human life — giving us food, medicine, and fermented products, while also causing infections, crop diseases, and food spoilage.
